meta.title: Optics Module 1 — Geometrical Optics
meta.subject: Physics · CU-FYUGP BSc Physics Honours Sem V (PHY5B08)

glossary.definition: Geometrical optics is the branch of optics that models light propagation in terms of rays by neglecting the finite wavelength of light in the limit where wavelength approaches zero.
glossary.example: Tracing light through lenses and mirrors whose dimensions are much larger than 0.00001 cm.

glossary.definition: A light ray is an infinitesimally thin pencil of light that defines the path of energy propagation in the limit as the optical wavelength approaches zero.
glossary.example: A straight beam of light travelling through uniform air.

glossary.definition: The refractive index of a medium is the dimensionless ratio of the speed of light in free space to the phase speed of light in that medium.
glossary.example: Crown glass with n = 1.5 slows light to two-thirds of its vacuum speed c.

glossary.definition: Optical path length is the geometric distance light travels multiplied by the refractive index of the medium, integrated along the trajectory between two points.
glossary.example: A 2 cm path in glass of refractive index 1.5 has an optical path length of 3 cm.

glossary.definition: Fermat's principle states that the actual ray path between two points is the trajectory for which the optical path length or travel time is stationary with respect to small path variations.
glossary.example: Light reflecting off a flat mirror at equal angles of incidence and reflection so the total path is minimized.

glossary.definition: A homogeneous medium is an optical region in which the refractive index has the same constant value at every point.
glossary.example: Still air at uniform temperature and pressure, where light rays travel in straight lines.

glossary.definition: An inhomogeneous medium is a material whose refractive index varies continuously with position, causing light rays to follow curved paths.
glossary.example: Air above hot asphalt on a sunny day, where density and refractive index increase with height and create a mirage.

glossary.definition: Snell's law is the refraction relation stating that the product of the local refractive index and the sine of the ray angle with the surface normal remains equal across an interface.
glossary.example: A ray passing from air (n = 1) into water (n = 1.33) bends closer to the normal.

glossary.definition: The paraxial approximation is the small-angle limit of ray optics in which rays make tiny angles with the optical axis, allowing sines and tangents of angles in radians to be replaced by the angles themselves.
glossary.example: Replacing sin phi with phi for rays striking near the vertex of a spherical lens.

glossary.definition: The Cartesian sign convention is the coordinate rule taking the surface vertex as origin with incident light travelling from left to right, making distances to the right and upward positive.
glossary.example: An object placed 40 cm to the left of a lens vertex has object distance u = -40 cm.

glossary.term: Gaussian formula for a single spherical surface
glossary.definition: The Gaussian formula for a single spherical surface is the paraxial refraction equation relating object distance, image distance, surface radius of curvature and the two refractive indices.
glossary.example: Calculating where a glass rod with a curved end focuses paraxial rays from an axial point.

glossary.definition: A meridional ray is a light ray that lies completely within a single plane containing the optical axis of the system.
glossary.example: Any ray emitted from an object point located directly on the optical axis.

glossary.definition: A skew ray is a non-planar light ray from an off-axis point that does not intersect the optical axis and does not remain confined to a single plane after refraction.
glossary.example: An off-axis ray entering a lens at an angle skew to the plane of the optical axis.

glossary.definition: The spherical mirror equation is the paraxial reflection relation stating that the sum of the reciprocals of object distance and image distance equals twice the reciprocal of the radius of curvature.
glossary.example: Finding the image position of an object in front of a concave mirror of radius R = -60 cm.

glossary.definition: A thin lens is a transparent medium bounded by two spherical refracting surfaces whose centre thickness is negligible compared with the radii of curvature and the object and image distances.
glossary.example: A laboratory glass spectacle lens whose thickness of a few millimetres is much smaller than its focal length.

glossary.definition: The thin lens formula is the paraxial equation linking the reciprocal image and object distances to the relative refractive index and the curvatures of the two lens surfaces.
glossary.example: Designing a biconvex glass lens of focal length +20 cm from its two surface radii.

glossary.definition: The first principal focus is the axial point such that rays passing through it, or directed toward it, emerge parallel to the optical axis after refraction through the lens.
glossary.example: Placing a point source at F1 of a converging lens to produce a collimated beam.

glossary.definition: The second principal focus is the axial point where incident rays travelling parallel to the optical axis intersect, or appear to diverge from, after refraction by the lens.
glossary.example: Parallel sunlight converging to a bright spot at F2 behind a magnifying glass.

glossary.definition: The Newtonian lens formula is the paraxial relation stating that the product of object distance from the first focus and image distance from the second focus equals the product of the two focal lengths.
glossary.example: If f = 10 cm in air and an object is 20 cm left of F1 (x1 = -20 cm), the image is at x2 = +5 cm right of F2.

glossary.definition: Lateral magnification is the dimensionless ratio of the transverse height of the image to the transverse height of the object measured perpendicular to the optical axis.
glossary.example: An image of height -2 cm formed from a 1 cm tall object has lateral magnification m = -2.

sheets.title: Fermat's principle & laws of rays
sheets.source: Ghatak, Optics (6th ed.), Chapter 3, Sections 3.1–3.2 (unit-1.pdf pp. 1–6 / book pp. 3.3–3.8).

cards.title: Why light picks a stationary time path
cards.meaning: Instead of testing every possible route by hand, Fermat's principle says light travels along a path whose travel time does not change to first order when you wiggle the path slightly.
cards.picture: Imagine walking from dry sand into shallow water to reach a buoy: going straight is too long in slow water, while walking too far along the beach adds extra sand distance; the fastest path bends at the shoreline.
cards.example: When light goes from air into glass of refractive index 1.5, it bends toward the normal so it spends less distance inside the slower glass.
cards.bridge: Formally, the travel time is the optical path integral divided by c, and setting its first variation to zero gives both the law of reflection and Snell's law of refraction.

cards.label: 01 · Definition
cards.title: What is geometrical optics?
cards.body: Geometrical optics is the zero-wavelength limit of optics (\(\lambda \to 0\)) in which diffraction vanishes and energy travels along infinitesimally thin pencils of light called rays.

cards.label: 02 · Definition
cards.title: What is Fermat's principle?
cards.body: Fermat's principle states that the actual ray path between two points is the one for which the optical path length \(\int n\,ds\) is stationary with respect to small path variations.

cards.label: 03 · Ray diagram
cards.title: Reflection and refraction from Fermat's principle
cards.body: For a plane mirror \(MN\), minimizing \(AP + PB = A'P + PB\) puts \(P\) on the straight line \(A'B\) so \(i = r\). Across an interface \(PQ\), stationarity gives Snell's law.
examples: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

ask.q: For all paraxial rays (any small \(\theta \neq 0\)) from \(O\) to focus at \(I\) where \(y = y_0\), what must hold?
options: Only \(\theta = 0\) can ever satisfy Fermat's principle
ask.why: When the bracket vanishes at \(y = y_0\), \(\frac{dL_{\text{op}}}{d\theta} = 0\) for every paraxial angle \(\theta\), so all paraxial rays take the same time.

Isolate the curvature term on one side.

ask.q: What does the second derivative \(\frac{d^2 L_{\text{op}}}{d\theta^2} = r^2 n_2\left(\frac{1}{y} - \frac{1}{y_0}\right)\) tell us about the axial ray \(OPQ\)?
options: It is a minimum for \(y < y_0\), stationary at \(y = y_0\), and a maximum for \(y > y_0\)
It is always a minimum for every point \(Q\)
It is always a maximum for every point \(Q\)
It vanishes everywhere along the axis
ask.why: For \(y > y_0\) (right of image \(I\)), \(\frac{d^2 L_{\text{op}}}{d\theta^2} < 0\) so \(OPQ\) is a local maximum; for \(y < y_0\) it is a minimum; at \(y = y_0\) it is stationary.

ask.q: Under the Cartesian sign convention for Fig. 3.10 (\(O\) on the left of \(P\), \(I\) and \(C\) on the right), what are the signs of \(u, v, R\)?
ask.why: Distances to the left of vertex \(P\) are negative and distances to the right of \(P\) are positive.

ask.q: When the refracted rays diverge from a virtual image \(I\) on the axis (Ghatak Example 3.4), which optical quantity is stationary?

cards.label: 05 · Definition
cards.title: What is an inhomogeneous medium?
cards.body: An inhomogeneous medium is a region where the refractive index \(n\) varies continuously with position, causing rays to bend along curved paths instead of straight lines.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: According to the modern, complete form of Fermat's principle, the actual ray path between two points is the one for which the optical path length is:
options: Stationary (a minimum, a maximum, or constant) with respect to path variations
Strictly the absolute minimum time for every optical system
Strictly a maximum whenever refraction occurs
Independent of the refractive index of the medium
cards.why: Fermat's original 'least time' statement was incomplete; the exact condition is \(\delta\int n\,ds = 0\), which includes minima, maxima and constant-time paths.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In an ellipsoidal reflector with foci \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), how does the travel time of rays leaving \(S_1\) and reflecting from different points \(P\) on the surface to \(S_2\) behave?
options: It is stationary with an identical constant value \(S_1P + S_2P = \text{const}\) for all points \(P\)
It is strictly smaller at the ends of the minor axis than elsewhere
It is strictly larger at the ends of the minor axis than elsewhere
cards.why: By definition of an ellipse, \(S_1P + S_2P\) is constant for every point \(P\) on the surface, so all rays from \(S_1\) take the exact same time to reach \(S_2\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: When the diameter of a circular aperture becomes very small (around \(0.1\text{ mm}\) or less), the light patch on a screen loses its sharp boundaries because of the wave phenomenon called ______.
cards.why: Diffraction arises from the finite wavelength \(\lambda\) of light and disappears only in the geometrical optics limit \(\lambda \to 0\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A light ray travels \(12\text{ cm}\) in air (\(n_1 = 1.0\)) and then \(10\text{ cm}\) inside glass (\(n_2 = 1.5\)). What is the total optical path length \(L_{\text{op}}\)?

sheets.title: Refraction & reflection at a sphere
sheets.source: Ghatak, Optics (6th ed.), Chapter 4, Eq. (4.1) and Sections 4.2–4.3 (unit-2.pdf pp. 1–3 / book pp. 4.2–4.4). Note: Section 4.1 introductory prose before Eq. (4.1) is not included in the provided unit files.

cards.title: Why only near-axis rays form a sharp point image
cards.meaning: A spherical surface does not focus wide-angle rays to a single point, but rays that stay close to the central axis all bend linearly with height and meet at one common image point.
cards.picture: Think of a small patch right at the pole of a globe: for tiny angles, the curve is gentle enough that sine, tangent, and the angle in radians are practically identical.
cards.example: At an angle of 0.05 radians (about 2.9 degrees), sin(0.05) = 0.04998 and tan(0.05) = 0.05004, so replacing both by 0.05 is accurate to better than 0.1%.
cards.bridge: Replacing sin(phi) and tan(phi) by phi lets the height h cancel out of Snell's law, so every paraxial ray from O intersects the axis at the same image distance v.

cards.label: 01 · Definition
cards.title: What is the paraxial approximation?
cards.body: The paraxial approximation is the small-angle regime in which rays make tiny angles with the optical axis so \(\sin\phi \approx \tan\phi \approx \phi\) (in radians), making all rays from \(O\) converge to one image point \(I\).

cards.label: 02 · Definition
cards.title: What is the Cartesian sign convention?
cards.body: The Cartesian sign convention places the origin at vertex \(P\) with incident rays coming from the left: distances to the right of \(P\) and upward from the axis are positive; to the left and downward are negative.
cards.tex: u < 0 \text{ (left of } P\text{)}, \qquad v > 0,\; R > 0 \text{ (right of } P\text{)}

cards.label: 03 · Ray diagram
cards.title: Refraction at a single spherical surface
cards.body: Surface \(SPM\) of radius \(R > 0\) separates \(n_1\) and \(n_2\). Exterior angles of triangles \(OSC\) and \(ISC\) give \(\phi_1 = \beta + \alpha_1\) and \(\phi_2 = \beta - \alpha_2\), with \(OD \approx OP = x\).

ask.q: In \(\triangle ISC\) of Fig. 4.1(a), how is the refraction angle \(\phi_2\) related to \(\beta\) and \(\alpha_2\)?
ask.why: Angle \(\beta\) at \(C\) is the exterior angle to \(\triangle ISC\), so \(\beta = \phi_2 + \alpha_2\), giving \(\phi_2 = \beta - \alpha_2\).

steps.note: Use paraxial Snell's law \(n_1\phi_1 = n_2\phi_2\) with \(\phi_2 = \frac{h}{r} - \frac{h}{y}\).

ask.q: Why does every paraxial ray from \(O\) focus at the same image distance \(y\) regardless of its height \(h\)?
options: Because \(h\) appears linearly in every term and cancels when we divide both sides by \(h\)
Because \(h\) is always equal to the radius \(r\)
ask.why: Dividing by \(h\) eliminates the ray height completely, leaving a single image distance \(y\) for all paraxial rays.

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(h\) and distribute \(n_1\) and \(n_2\).
Collect distance terms on the left and curvature terms on the right (Ghatak Eq. 4.4).

ask.q: For the ray diagram of Fig. 4.1(a), how do the signed quantities \(u, v, R\) relate to the positive lengths \(x, y, r\)?
ask.why: Object \(O\) is to the left of vertex \(P\) (\(u = -x\)), while image \(I\) and centre \(C\) are to the right of \(P\) (\(v = y, R = r\)).

steps.note: Gaussian formula for a single spherical surface (Ghatak Eq. 4.5).

ask.q: When is the object distance \(u\) positive for a refracting surface?
options: When incident rays from the left are already converging toward a virtual object point to the right of \(P\)
Whenever the real object is placed further than \(2R\) to the left of \(P\)
Never; \(u\) is negative for all optical systems
ask.why: As shown in Ghatak Fig. 4.1(b) and Example 4.1, \(u > 0\) when incident rays converge toward a point on the right of the surface.

cards.label: 04 · Definition
cards.title: What are meridional and skew rays?
cards.body: A meridional ray is a ray confined to a single plane containing the optical axis (line joining \(C_1\) and \(C_2\)), whereas a skew ray from an off-axis point neither intersects the axis nor stays in one plane.

cards.label: 05 · Ray diagram
cards.title: Reflection by a single spherical surface
cards.body: For a concave spherical mirror \(SPM\) with \(O, C, I\) on the left of \(P\), \(\phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1\) and \(\phi_2 = \alpha_2 - \beta\). Setting \(\phi_1 = \phi_2\) and \(u = -x, v = -y, R = -r\) gives the mirror equation.

cards.title: Spherical mirror equation from paraxial reflection
cards.legend: Magnitudes \(x = OP\), \(y = IP\), \(r = CP\), ray height \(h = SD\) (Ghatak Section 4.3).

phases.name: Angles
phases.why: relate incidence and reflection angles to α1, β, α2

phases.name: Reflection law
phases.why: set φ1 = φ2 and cancel h

phases.name: Sign convention
phases.why: substitute u = -x, v = -y, R = -r

steps.note: In \(\triangle OSC\) (Fig. 4.3), \(\beta = \alpha_1 + \phi_1\), so \(\phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1 \approx \frac{h}{r} - \frac{h}{x}\).
By the law of reflection \(\phi_1 = \phi_2\), where \(\phi_2 = \alpha_2 - \beta \approx \frac{h}{y} - \frac{h}{r}\).

ask.q: In \(\triangle CSI\) of Fig. 4.3, why is \(\phi_2 = \alpha_2 - \beta\)?
options: Because \(\alpha_2\) at \(I\) is the exterior angle to \(\triangle CSI\), so \(\alpha_2 = \beta + \phi_2\)
Because \(\beta\) is the exterior angle to \(\triangle CSI\)
Because \(C\) lies to the right of \(I\)
ask.why: Point \(I\) lies between \(C\) and \(P\), making \(\alpha_2\) the exterior angle of \(\triangle CSI\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by the common height \(h\).
Collect \(x, y\) on the left and \(r\) on the right (Ghatak Eq. 4.6).

ask.q: Since \(O, C, I\) all lie to the left of vertex \(P\) in Fig. 4.3, how are \(u, v, R\) related to the positive lengths \(x, y, r\)?
ask.why: Every point to the left of the mirror vertex \(P\) has a negative coordinate.

steps.note: Replace the positive magnitudes \(x, y, r\) by \(-u, -v, -R\).

ask.q: How do we simplify \(-\frac{1}{u} - \frac{1}{v} = -\frac{2}{R}\) into the standard mirror equation?
options: Take the reciprocal of each term
ask.why: Multiplying both sides by \(-1\) makes every term positive in symbolic form.

steps.note: The spherical mirror equation (Ghatak Eq. 4.7).

ask.q: Which formal substitution in the single-surface refraction formula \(\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\) directly yields the mirror equation?
ask.why: Setting \(n_2 = -n_1\) turns Snell's law \(n_1\sin\phi_1 = n_2\sin\phi_2\) into the reflection law and converts Eq. (4.5) into \(\frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{2}{R}\).

cards.title: Two-surface glass block & two-mirror system
cards.tex: \text{Ex. 4.1: } \frac{1.5}{v_1} + \frac{1}{40} = \frac{0.5}{15} \Rightarrow v_1 = +180\text{ cm}, \quad u_2 = 180 - 30 = +150\text{ cm} \Rightarrow v = +33\tfrac{1}{3}\text{ cm}
cards.body: Ghatak Ex. 4.1: A \(30\text{ cm}\) medium (\(n = 1.5\), \(R_1 = +15\text{ cm}\), \(R_2 = -25\text{ cm}\)) images \(u_1 = -40\text{ cm}\) at \(v_1 = +180\text{ cm}\), giving virtual object \(u_2 = +150\text{ cm}\) and real image \(v = +33\tfrac{1}{3}\text{ cm}\). Ex. 4.2: Concave mirror (\(R_1 = -60\text{ cm}\), \(u_1 = -80\text{ cm}\)) gives \(v_1 = -48\text{ cm}\); for convex mirror \(40\text{ cm}\) left (\(R_2 = -20\text{ cm}\)), \(u_2 = -8\text{ cm}\) gives \(v_2 = +40\text{ cm}\) at \(P_1\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Under the Cartesian sign convention used in Ghatak, when is the angle that a ray makes with the optical axis positive?
options: When the axis must be rotated anticlockwise through the acute angle to coincide with the ray
When the axis must be rotated clockwise through the acute angle to coincide with the ray
Whenever the ray is above the optical axis
Whenever the ray travels from left to right
cards.why: By Rule 3 of Section 4.2.1, anticlockwise acute rotation from the axis (or normal) to the ray is positive, and clockwise is negative.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Rays from an off-axis point that do not intersect the optical axis and do not remain confined to a single plane after refraction at a second surface are called ______ rays.
cards.why: Rays confined to a plane containing the optical axis are meridional rays, whereas non-planar off-axis rays are skew rays.

sections.title: Thin Lenses, Principal Foci and Magnification

sheets.title: Thin lenses & principal foci
sheets.source: Ghatak, Optics (6th ed.), Chapter 4, Sections 4.4–4.5 (unit-3.pdf pp. 1–2 / book pp. 4.5–4.6).

cards.title: Why two spherical surfaces act as one focal power
cards.meaning: A thin lens bends light twice—once entering the front surface and once leaving the back surface—with the two vertices so close together that both distances are measured from the same centre point P.
cards.picture: Picture a relay race with zero handoff distance: the first surface aims rays toward an intermediate image Q at distance v', and the second surface immediately intercepts those rays and redirects them to the final image I at v.
cards.example: In a biconvex glass lens in air (R1 > 0, R2 < 0), both the front convex surface and the back surface bend rays toward the axis, so their converging powers add together.
cards.bridge: Adding the two single-surface Gaussian equations cancels the intermediate image distance v' and yields the thin lens formula.

cards.label: 01 · Definition
cards.title: What is a thin lens?
cards.body: A thin lens is a medium bounded by two spherical refracting surfaces whose thickness \(t\) is very small compared with the object and image distances and the radii of curvature \(R_1\) and \(R_2\).

cards.label: 02 · Ray diagram
cards.title: Image formation & surrounding medium effect
cards.body: The first surface forms an intermediate image at \(Q\) (distance \(v'\)), which acts as a virtual object for the second surface to form final image \(I\) at \(v\). If \(n_2 < n_1\), a biconvex lens diverges!

cards.title: Thin lens & lensmaker's formula by two refractions
cards.legend: Surrounding medium \(n_1\), lens index \(n_2\), relative index \(n = \frac{n_2}{n_1}\), radii \(R_1, R_2\), intermediate image distance \(v'\).

phases.name: Two surfaces
phases.why: write single-surface Gaussian equations for R1 and R2

phases.name: Combine
phases.why: add the two equations to eliminate intermediate image v'

phases.name: Focal length
phases.why: divide by n1 and define n = n2/n1 and focal length f

steps.note: Refraction at the first surface of radius \(R_1\) forms an image at \(v'\) (Ghatak Eq. 4.8).
Add the second surface equation \(\frac{n_1}{v} - \frac{n_2}{v'} = \frac{n_1 - n_2}{R_2}\); \(\frac{n_2}{v'}\) cancels!

ask.q: Why can we use the same intermediate distance \(v'\) for the second surface without subtracting the lens thickness \(t\)?
options: Because the lens is assumed thin (\(t \ll |u|, |v|, |R_1|, |R_2|\)), so all distances are measured from the common centre \(P\)
Because light travels instantaneously inside the glass
Because \(R_1 = R_2\) for every thin lens
ask.why: In the thin-lens approximation, the two surface vertices coincide with the lens centre \(P\).

steps.note: Factor \(n_1\) on the left and \(n_2 - n_1\) on the right (since \(n_1 - n_2 = -(n_2 - n_1)\)).

ask.q: Why does the second curvature term have a minus sign \(-\frac{1}{R_2}\) after factoring out \((n_2 - n_1)\)?
options: At the second surface light passes from \(n_2\) back into \(n_1\), so the numerator is \(n_1 - n_2 = -(n_2 - n_1)\)
Because the second surface reflects light
ask.why: Interchanging the initial and final media at the exit surface reverses \(n_2 - n_1\) to \(n_1 - n_2\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(n_1\).
Thin lens formula with relative refractive index \(n = \frac{n_2}{n_1}\) (Ghatak Eq. 4.10).

ask.q: For a biconvex lens (\(R_1 > 0, R_2 < 0\)) immersed in a liquid of refractive index \(n_1 > n_2\), what is the sign of \(f\)?
options: Negative (\(f < 0\)), so the biconvex lens acts as a diverging lens

steps.note: Gaussian form of the thin lens formula (Ghatak Eqs. 4.11–4.12).

ask.q: For a biconcave lens in air (\(n > 1\)), what are the signs of \(R_1\), \(R_2\), and \(f\)?
ask.why: As shown in Fig. 4.6(b), the left concave surface has its centre on the left (\(R_1 < 0\)) and the right surface has its centre on the right (\(R_2 > 0\)), so \(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2} < 0\) and \(f < 0\).

cards.label: 03 · Definition
cards.title: What are the first and second principal foci?
cards.body: The first principal focus \(F_1\) (at \(u = f_1\)) is the axial point whose rays emerge parallel to the axis (\(v = \infty\)); the second principal focus \(F_2\) (at \(v = f_2\)) is where rays parallel to the axis (\(u = -\infty\)) focus.

cards.label: 04 · Ray diagram
cards.title: Three principal rays for graphical construction
cards.body: (i) Ray 1 through \(F_1\) emerges parallel to the axis. (ii) Ray 2 parallel to the axis passes through \(F_2\). (iii) Ray 3 through lens centre \(P\) passes undeviated (since \(u = 0 \Rightarrow v = 0\)).

cards.title: First and second focal lengths for different media
cards.legend: Left medium \(n_1\), lens medium \(n_2\), right medium \(n_3\), radii \(R_1, R_2\) (Ghatak Eqs. 4.14–4.16).

phases.name: General lens
phases.why: combine refractions when left and right media have indices n1 and n3

phases.name: First focus
phases.why: set v = ∞ to find first focal length f1

phases.name: Second focus
phases.why: set u = -∞ to find second focal length f2 and compare

steps.note: General thin lens equation when media on the two sides are \(n_1\) and \(n_3\) (Ghatak Eq. 4.14).
For the first principal focus \(F_1\), emergent rays are parallel to the axis (\(v = \infty\)).

ask.q: What condition defines the first focal length \(u = f_1\) of a lens?
options: Rays passing through (or directed toward) \(F_1\) emerge parallel to the axis, so \(v = \infty\)
Incident rays are parallel to the axis, so \(u = -\infty\)
Object and image have equal size, so \(v = u\)
The ray passes undeviated through \(P\), so \(u = 0\)
ask.why: By definition of the first principal focus (Ray 1 in Fig. 4.8), when \(u = f_1\), the refracted ray emerges parallel to the axis (\(v = \infty\)).

steps.note: First focal length formula for general media (Ghatak Eq. 4.15).
For the second principal focus \(F_2\), incident rays are parallel to the axis (\(u = -\infty\)).

ask.q: What condition defines the second focal length \(v = f_2\) of a lens?
options: Incident rays travel parallel to the axis (\(u = -\infty\)) and intersect (or appear to diverge from) \(F_2\)
Emergent rays travel parallel to the axis (\(v = \infty\))
The image forms at the centre of curvature \(C_2\)
ask.why: By definition of the second principal focus (Ray 2 in Fig. 4.8), when \(u = -\infty\), the image distance is \(v = f_2\).

steps.note: Second focal length formula for general media (Ghatak Eq. 4.16).

ask.q: Comparing the formulas for \(f_1\) and \(f_2\), what is the ratio \(\frac{f_2}{f_1}\) when \(n_3 \neq n_1\)?
ask.why: Since \(-\frac{n_1}{f_1} = \frac{n_3}{f_2}\), the ratio of the two focal lengths is \(\frac{f_2}{f_1} = -\frac{n_3}{n_1}\).

steps.note: When the medium on both sides is identical (\(n_3 = n_1\)), \(f_2 = -f_1 = f\) (Ghatak Eq. 4.13).

ask.q: For a diverging lens in air, what are the signs of the first focal length \(f_1\) and the second focal length \(f_2\)?
ask.why: As shown in Fig. 4.8(b), for a diverging lens \(F_1\) lies on the right of \(P\) (\(f_1 > 0\)) and \(F_2\) lies on the left of \(P\) (\(f_2 < 0\)).

cards.label: 05 · Worked example
cards.title: Focal length of a biconvex lens in air
cards.body: For a glass biconvex lens (\(n = 1.5\)) in air with radii \(R_1 = +15\text{ cm}\) and \(R_2 = -30\text{ cm}\), the second focal length is \(f_2 = f = +20\text{ cm}\) and the first focal length is \(f_1 = -20\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why does a paraxial ray passing through the optical centre \(P\) of a thin lens emerge undeviated?
options: Because for a thin lens, setting \(u = 0\) in the thin lens formula gives \(v = 0\)
Because the refractive index at the centre \(P\) is equal to 1
Because total internal reflection occurs at \(P\)
cards.why: As noted in the footnote of Ghatak Section 4.5, \(\frac{n_3}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \text{const}\) implies that as \(u \to 0\), \(v \to 0\) with unit slope magnification.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: A glass biconcave lens (\(n_2 = 1.5\)) is placed inside a dense liquid of refractive index \(n_1 = 1.75\). How does the lens behave?
options: As a plane glass plate with \(f = \infty\)
cards.why: For a biconcave lens \(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2} < 0\), and since \(n_2 < n_1\) we also have \(\frac{n_2}{n_1} - 1 < 0\); the product of two negative factors gives \(\frac{1}{f} > 0\) (Fig. 4.7d).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: For a converging lens in air, the first focal length \(f_1\) is negative and the second focal length \(f_2\) is ______.
cards.why: Parallel rays from the left converge to \(F_2\) on the right of a converging lens, so \(f_2 > 0\) while \(f_1 = -f_2 < 0\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: An equiconvex lens of refractive index \(n = 1.5\) in air has radii \(R_1 = +20\text{ cm}\) and \(R_2 = -20\text{ cm}\). What is its focal length \(f\)?

sheets.title: Newton's formula & magnification
sheets.source: Ghatak, Optics (6th ed.), Chapter 4, Sections 4.6–4.7 (unit-4.pdf pp. 1–2 / book pp. 4.7–4.8).

cards.title: Measuring object and image from the foci instead of the lens
cards.meaning: Instead of measuring u and v from the lens centre P, Newton's formula measures how far the object is from the first focus F1 (x1) and how far the image is from the second focus F2 (x2).
cards.picture: As you push an object further left past F1 (making |x1| larger), the image moves closer to F2 on the right (making |x2| smaller) so their product stays locked at f^2.
cards.example: For a lens of focal length f = 10 cm, an object 20 cm left of F1 (x1 = -20 cm) forms an image at x2 = -f^2 / x1 = -100 / (-20) = +5 cm to the right of F2.
cards.bridge: Comparing the two pairs of similar right triangles formed by Ray 1 at F1 and Ray 2 at F2 equates both ratios to -y'/y and gives f1 f2 = x1 x2.

cards.label: 01 · Definition
cards.title: What is the Newtonian lens formula?
cards.body: The Newtonian lens formula relates the object distance \(x_1\) from the first principal focus \(F_1\) and the image distance \(x_2\) from the second principal focus \(F_2\) by \(f_1 f_2 = x_1 x_2\) (or \(x_1 x_2 = -f^2\) in a uniform medium).
cards.tex: f_1 f_2 = x_1 x_2, \qquad x_1 x_2 = -f^2 \quad (\text{when } n_3 = n_1)
examples: x₁ and x₂ have opposite signs

cards.title: Similar triangles for Newton's formula

ask.q: In Fig. 4.8(a), why is the vertical side of \(\triangle PLF_1\) and \(\triangle BIF_2\) written as \(-y'\)?
options: Because the image is inverted below the axis (\(y' < 0\)), so its positive geometric length is \(-y'\)
Because the object height \(y\) is negative
Because \(f_2\) is negative for a converging lens
Because rays travel from right to left
ask.why: Vertical distances below the axis are negative (\(y' < 0\)), so the positive triangle side length is \(-y'\).

ask.q: For a diverging lens in Fig. 4.8(b), the similar-triangle ratios read \(\frac{y'}{y} = \frac{f_1}{-x_1} = \frac{-x_2}{-f_2}\). Does this change the relation between \(x_1, x_2, f_1, f_2\)?

Yes; the sign of \(x_1 x_2\) reverses for a diverging lens
Yes; \(f_1 f_2 = -x_1 x_2\) for a diverging lens

ask.q: What does \(x_1 x_2 = -f^2 < 0\) tell us about the positions of the object and image relative to \(F_1\) and \(F_2\)?
options: \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) must have opposite signs: if the object is to the left of \(F_1\), the image is to the right of \(F_2\), and vice versa
\(x_1\) and \(x_2\) always have the same sign
The image always lies between \(F_1\) and \(F_2\)
The focal length \(f\) must be imaginary
ask.why: Since \(-f^2\) is always negative, \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) must have opposite signs.

cards.label: 03 · Definition
cards.title: What is lateral magnification?
cards.body: Lateral magnification \(m\) is the ratio of the image height \(y'\) to the object height \(y\): for a thin lens in one medium, \(m = \frac{y'}{y} = \frac{v}{u} = -\frac{f_1}{x_1} = -\frac{x_2}{f_2}\).

cards.title: Lateral magnification of a surface and a thin lens
cards.legend: Object height \(y\), image height \(y'\), surface radius \(R\), indices \(n_1, n_2\), intermediate image \(v'\) (Ghatak Eqs. 4.22–4.24).

Divide the top and bottom of the right-hand fraction by \(R\).

ask.q: Multiplying the Gaussian surface equation \(\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\) by \(v\) or \(u\) gives expressions for \(\frac{v}{R} - 1\) and \(-\frac{u}{R} + 1\). What is \(\frac{n_2 - n_1}{n_1}\frac{v}{R}\)?
ask.why: As shown below Eq. (4.22) in Ghatak, multiplying Eq. (4.5) by \(\frac{v}{n_1}\) gives \(\frac{n_2}{n_1} - \frac{v}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{n_1}\frac{v}{R}\).

steps.note: Substitute for \(v/R\) and \(u/R\) using Eq. (4.5) and negate (Ghatak Eq. 4.23).

ask.q: For the first surface of a thin lens (\(n_1 \to n_2\), object at \(u\), intermediate image at \(v'\)), what is its lateral magnification \(m_1\)?
ask.why: Applying Eq. (4.23) to the first surface with image distance \(v'\) directly gives \(m_1 = \frac{n_1 v'}{n_2 u}\).

move.by: m = m_1 m_2 \text{ with } m_1 = \frac{n_1 v'}{n_2 u}, \; m_2 = \frac{n_2 v}{n_1 v'}

steps.note: Total magnification is the product of the two surface magnifications \(m_1 m_2\).

ask.q: What happens to the refractive indices \(n_1, n_2\) and the intermediate image distance \(v'\) when \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are multiplied?
ask.why: Because the light returns to medium \(n_1\) and the intermediate image at \(v'\) is the object for the second surface, both factors cancel.

steps.note: Lateral magnification of a thin lens with the same medium on both sides (Ghatak Eq. 4.24).

ask.q: If a two-lens system has first-lens magnification \(m_1 = -1\) and second-lens magnification \(m_2 = -\frac{5}{11}\), what is the overall magnification \(m = m_1 m_2\)?
ask.why: Multiplying two negative magnifications gives a positive overall magnification \(m = (-1)\left(-\frac{5}{11}\right) = +\frac{5}{11}\).

cards.title: Position and size of image in Example 4.3
cards.body: For lens 1 (\(f_1 = +20\text{ cm}, u_1 = -40\text{ cm}\)), \(v_1 = +40\text{ cm}\) and \(m_1 = \frac{40}{-40} = -1\). Lens 2 sits \(8\text{ cm}\) to the right, so \(u_2 = 40 - 8 = +32\text{ cm}\); with \(f_2 = -10\text{ cm}\), \(v_2 \approx -14.5\text{ cm}\) and height \(y' = +0.455\text{ cm}\) (virtual, erect).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For a single spherical refracting surface separating media of refractive indices \(n_1\) and \(n_2\), what is the lateral magnification \(m = \frac{y'}{y}\)?
cards.why: By Eq. (4.23), similar triangles at the centre of curvature \(C\) combined with the Gaussian surface equation yield \(m = \frac{n_1 v}{n_2 u}\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: If the lateral magnification \(m\) of an optical image is negative (\(m < 0\)), the image is ______ relative to the object.
cards.why: Since \(m = \frac{y'}{y}\), a negative value means \(y'\) and \(y\) have opposite signs, so the image is inverted.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A thin converging lens in air has focal length \(f = 15\text{ cm}\). If an object lies \(25\text{ cm}\) to the left of the first principal focus \(F_1\) (so \(x_1 = -25\text{ cm}\)), find its image distance \(x_2\) from the second principal focus \(F_2\).
cards.why: Using Newton's formula \(x_1 x_2 = -f^2\): \((-25)x_2 = -(15)^2 = -225\), giving \(x_2 = +9\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In Ghatak Example 4.3, the first lens forms an image at \(v_1 = +40\text{ cm}\) to its right. A second lens is placed \(8\text{ cm}\) to the right of the first lens. What is the virtual object distance \(u_2\) for the second lens?
cards.why: Measured from the second lens (which is \(8\text{ cm}\) to the right of the first lens), the converging rays aim toward a point \(40 - 8 = +32\text{ cm}\) to the right.
